title: Genesis 4. The Cup Rejected.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 4. The Cup Rejected.
Eve bears a son.
She says: I have gotten a man with the Lord.
She bears another, Abel.
Abel keeps sheep.
Cain works the ground.
Time passes.
Cain brings an offering from the fruit of the ground.
Abel brings the firstborn of his flock, and their fat.
God looks at Abel and his offering.
He does not look at Cain and his offering.
The text does not fully explain why.
It simply says God received one and not the other.
The first act of worship in Scripture is also the first act of rejection.
The Cup is offered and refused.
Cain's face falls.
God speaks to Cain: Why are you angry?
Why has your face fallen?
If you do well, will you not be accepted?
If you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door.
Its desire is for you.
But you must rule over it.
This is the first time sin is named.
Not as something already committed, but as something crouching.
Waiting at the threshold.
God tells Cain he can rule over it.
The boundary that was set inside abundance in chapter two is now spoken as a warning outside a closed door.
Sin is not yet inside.
But it is at the entrance.
Cain does not rule over it.
He speaks to Abel, his brother.
They go into a field.
And Cain rises against Abel his brother, and kills him.
The first brother story in Scripture.
It ends in blood.
Every brother story in Genesis will carry this wound, Isaac and Ishmael,
Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers, until chapter thirty-three,
when Esau runs to meet Jacob and the pattern breaks for the first time.
But here, at the beginning, the first brother kills the second.
God asks: Where is Abel your brother?
Cain answers: I do not know.
Am I my brother's keeper?
The first question a human asks God is a deflection.
As the man blamed the woman in chapter three,
Cain now erases Abel.
The Cup that was shared in chapter two and drained in chapter three is now filled with blood,
not God's covering, but man's violence.
God answers with the blood: What have you done?
The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.
The ground that was cursed for Adam's sake is now cursed again,
because it has opened its mouth to receive Abel's blood from Cain's hand.
When Cain works it, it will no longer give its strength.
He will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.
Cain says: My punishment is greater than I can bear.
You have driven me from the ground.
I will be hidden from Your face.
Whoever finds me will kill me.
God puts a mark on Cain.
A sign, so that anyone who finds him will not strike him.
Vengeance will be taken sevenfold on anyone who kills him.
The one who shed blood is protected by the God whose boundary he crossed.
The Cup is rejected, filled with blood, and then, inside the judgment,
preserved.
Cain is marked, not destroyed.
Cain leaves the presence of the Lord.
He settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
He knows his wife.
She bears Enoch.
He builds a city and names it after his son.
The first exile builds the first city.
The man who would not stay in the field with his brother builds walls.
The wanderer settles.
The one who fled God's presence constructs a place to belong that is not God's presence.
The line extends.
Enoch fathers Irad.
Irad fathers Mehujael.
Mehujael fathers Methushael.
Methushael fathers Lamech.
Lamech takes two wives, Adah and Zillah.
Adah bears Jabal,
the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.
His brother is Jubal,
the father of all who handle the harp and pipe.
Zillah bears Tubal-cain,
the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron.
The city produces culture.
Music, metallurgy, herding, craft.
The line of the exiled produces what looks like civilization.
The Cup that was rejected still pours,
but into vessels that do not acknowledge the hand that filled them.
Then Lamech speaks to his wives: Adah and Zillah, hear my voice.
You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech.
For I have slain a man for wounding me,
a young man for bruising me.
If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.
The seventh generation from Cain takes the mark of protection God gave a murderer and turns it into a boast.
The boundary God set to preserve life becomes, in Lamech's mouth,
a license to kill.
The Cup's protection has been seized and weaponized by the one it was meant to restrain.
Then Adam knows his wife again.
She bears a son and names him Seth:
For God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel,
since Cain killed him.
Seth has a son.
He names him Enosh.
At that time,
people began to call upon the name of the Lord.
The Cup, rejected and bloodied, begins to be refilled.
Not through Cain's city.
Not through Lamech's boast.
Through a line that turns back toward the One who asked:
Where is your brother?
and receives, instead of a deflection, a cry.
The first worship since the garden is not an offering of fruit or flock.
It is a calling on the name of the Lord.
What began in rest, ruptured in grabbing, drained in taking,
and filled with blood now carries a narrow thread:
a people who call.
The seed of the woman promised in chapter three has not yet appeared.
But the line that will carry the promise has begun.
